newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey paper attack fuels government-media row.
newsitem.headline: Turkey paper attack fuels government-media row.

text.p: A young man with apparent Islamist leanings attacked the headquarters of the secularist Turkish newspaper Hurriyet on Monday for delivering what he called "a blow to Islam," witnesses said.
The incident, the latest involving violence against Turkish media, reignited a war of words between the mainstream news organisations and the Islamist-led government.
Hurriyet editor Ertugrul Ozkok told reporters the attacker overpowered a guard, grabbed his gun and later shot a cleaner in the leg.
The cleaner, who was not seriously injured, said the man was apparently looking for owner Aydin Dogan, head of the media group Dogan Holding, because he had "dealt a blow" to Islam.
The state-run Anatolian news agency identified the assailant, who surrendered to police, as Huseyin Vuran, 22, a former student of Islamic studies.
Leading media figures were quick to point a finger at the ruling alliance of islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan and conservative leader Tansu Ciller over criticism of the media.

"It is a fact that members of the government have increased their statements targeting the Turkish media over the past few days," Ozkok said. "Such things create an atmosphere in which unpleasant incidents take place," he said.
Erbakan has never had an easy ride with the mainstream secularist media, which has taken a leading role in a row between the government and the strongly secularist army over Islamist activism.
Major newspapers have speculated with glee over the possibility that the army may stage its fourth coup since 1960.

In what the media viewed as a retort by Erbakan, the Islamist-held justice ministry ordered inquiries into eight journalists and two union officials for articles or speeches alleged to have been intended to provoke a military coup.
But, despite the attacker's apparent Islamist leanings, Ciller -- leader of the coalition's secularist conservatives -- took the brunt of the latest criticism.

Ozkok was joined by others in comparing Monday's attack with one 10 days ago on the offices of Flash TV, staged in an apparent reaction to a programme on organised crime in which a gangster accused top secular political figures of corruption.

"It is worrying to observe the extent of these attacks by urban guerrillas who are encouraged by the government's recent attitude against the media, and particularly by...Tansu Ciller's open targeting of media groups by announcing their names," said Press Council general secretary Nilufer Yalcin.

Ciller, who has been under attack from the media since she joined with Erbakan's Welfare Party in June, on Saturday accused the media of turning against her because she cut their incentive loans from state banks while prime minister.

She said that Dogan Holding, which owns Hurriyet, another daily, Milliyet and Kanal D television channel, had obtained $424.8 million between 1980 and 1994, when she cut off the funding. The rival Medya Holding had been given $200.4 million in the same period, she told a party rally.
She said Koc Holding, which is close to Dogan Holding, had also taken advantage of the incentives.
The major business group TUSIAD attacked Ciller for making "warped" statements, calling her "a politician who is leading Turkey into darkness."
Newspapers wrote a frenzy of editorials to counter Ciller's claims, saying the numbers were exaggerated and the loans were obtained legally.
"The people know very well who is gobbling up their money," said an editorial on Monday in Sabah daily, owned by Medya Holding and an erstwhile Ciller ally.
